key: Therefore he who would administer the kingdom, honouring it as he honours his own person, may be employed to govern it, and he who would administer it with the love which he bears to his own person may be entrusted with it.
s: The chapter says the kingdom may be entrusted to one who honours and loves it as his own person; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 13, takes the honouring as a ruler prizing himself and scorning others, who holds it only for a time, and the loving as one loving himself for the people’s sake, who lasts without blame.
src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 13, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

opened.locator: chapter 13 (厭恥), comments on 故貴以身為天下者，則可寄天下 and 愛以身為天下，若可託天下

evidence.words: 言人君貴其身而賤人，欲為天下主者，則可寄立，不可以久也。…言人君能愛其身，非為己也，乃欲為萬民之父母。以此得為天下主者，乃可以託其身於萬民之上，長無咎也。
evidence.gloss: It says: a ruler who prizes his own person and holds others cheap, wishing to be master of the world, may be set in place for a time, but cannot last. … It says: a ruler who can love his own person, not for his own sake but wishing to be father and mother to the myriad people, and who so becomes master of the world, may entrust his person above the myriad people and long be without blame.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref Tao Te Ching 13, at [12]). The Heshang Gong commentary comments on exactly these two lines of its base text (故貴以身為天下者，則可寄天下 / 愛以身為天下，若可託天下), which match the day’s chapter; it reads the first as a ruler who prizes himself and scorns others and holds power only provisionally (可寄立，不可以久也), the second as one who loves his person for the people’s sake and lasts without blame (長無咎也). Legge’s note independently confirms the commentary distinguishes the two characters. The sentence names the commentary’s contrast without adding to it; plain sense restates Legge’s verse without his parentheses. entry-check ok.
